title: Senate panel advances bill limiting times youth are automatically charged as adults
summary: A Senate committee gave overwhelming approval Friday to a bill that would reduce the number of crimes for which a youth would be automatically charged as an adult,  a proposal that’s been worked on for more than a decade.
content:
by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters February 27, 2026

by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters February 27, 2026

A Senate committee gave overwhelming approval Friday to a bill that would reduce the number of crimes for which a youth would be automatically charged as an adult,  a proposal that’s been worked on for more than a decade.

The Senate Judicial Proceedings Committee voted 10-1 for Senate Bill 323, which could be debated by the full Senate as soon as next week.

“I think it’s great that it’s happening on the last two days of Black History Month, but I think it’s been the product of a lot of work, a lot of reform within the juvenile system,” said Sen. William C. Smith Jr. (D-Montgomery), before Friday’s vote. Smith is chair of Judicial Proceedings and a sponsor of SB 323.

In general, the bill would raise the age at which a juvenile would be tried as an adult, from 14 in the current law to 16. It would also eliminate a number of crimes for which 16-year-olds are currently made eligible to be charge as adults. It doesn’t fully end the state’s practice of automatically charging youth as adults: 14- and 15-year-olds charged with first-degree murder or rape would still go straight to adult court.

Two Republicans – Sens. Chris West (R-Baltimore and Carroll) and Mike McKay (R-Western Maryland) – joined their eight Democratic colleagues to advance the bill.

Sen. William G. Folden (R-Frederick) was the only senator to vote no. The main message from Folden, a retired law enforcement officer: “Accountability matters.”

He read the headlines from a number of recent cases in which teens had access to guns and were charged in attacks and murders, including the case of a Prince George’s County 17-year-old charged, with three others, in the murder of a 14-year-old missing from Washington, D.C. In another case, Folden showed a picture of an assault rifle used in a crime by a 16-year-old.

“These aren’t childlike actions. These are adult actions that require adult consequences and accountability,” Folden said. “We are doing nothing for our victims and everything for our suspects in crime.”

The bill also proposes for the state’s Department of Juvenile Services temporarily detain children at least 16 years or older who are accused of gun offenses.

The bill was also amended to include language from Senate Bill 296, sponsored by Sen. Sara Love (D-Montgomery County), that prohibits youth who are charged as adults from being “detained or confined” in an adult prison. That provision would not take effect until October 2029, while the rest of the will would take effect on Oct. 1 of this year.

Juvenile Services Secretary Betsy Fox Tolentino — whose nomination was confirmed earlier Friday by the full Senate, removing the label “acting” from her title — had testified earlier this month in support of both SB 323 and the House version of the bill, sponsored by Del. J. Sandy Bartlett (D-Anne Arundel), who chairs the Judiciary Committee. Fox Tolentino was on hand before the Judicial Proceedings Committee vote Friday.

“We have a lot in front us, and we’re going to continue to build out our continuum for young people,” Fox Tolentino said before the voting session. “We’re going to continue to support our frontline workers. We’re going to continue to build a better system for our young people and our communities.”

Smith said at a panel discussion in Georgetown in November that about 85% of cases when youth are charged as adults are either dismissed or sent back down to juvenile court.

West, a co-sponsor of the bill, reiterated Friday how the bill can shorten the process for various offenses that go to adult court and eventually revert to juvenile court. The bill would allow a judge to decide where a case belongs quicker, but it also permits a state’s attorney “the right to try to move the case back to adult court.”

“We’re going to save these juveniles, who spend up to a year twiddling their fingers in limbo waiting for a decision about whether the case is going to move back to the juvenile court, which almost invariably happens,” West said. “We’re going to get those people the services they need early on rather than a year after the fact.”
